sections.title: How to choose and run a classroom game

blocks.x: Games work best when they practise one clear language aim. These activities are well-known classroom techniques used by English teachers around the world; the descriptions and examples here are written for this app. Each game page shows the skills, level, time, group size and materials, then how to play, examples you can copy, and variations.
Match the game to your goal

head: Your goal
Games to try
rows: Simon Says, Two Truths and a Lie, Find Someone Who, Learning Names, Stand in a Line
Charades, 20 Questions, Hot Seat, Taboo, Spot the Difference, Story Chain, Liar!, Slowly Reveal a Picture, What Would You Take?
Bingo, Word Chain, Odd One Out, Memory, Board Race, Stop the Bus, Kim's Memory Game, Feely Game, Mime an Adverb
Sentence Auction, Error Correction Relay, Scrambled Sentences, Market Memory Chain, Alibis, Paper Fortune-Teller, Where's the Mouse?
Running Dictation, Telephone, Listen and Draw, Repeat It If It Is True, Listen for the Difference, Act Out a Story, Put the Story in Order
True and False Sentences, Story Consequences, Bouncing Stories, What's in His Pocket?
Hangman, Running Dictation, Stop the Bus
Word Sun, Mind Map, Folding Vocabulary Book
Review at the end of a unit

items: Explain the rules in simple English and show one example round before you start.
Say the language aim first, so learners know what to use (for example, past simple questions).
Set a visible time limit and keep the game short: 10 to 15 minutes is usually enough.
Use mixed-level teams so stronger learners help weaker ones.
Give every learner a job (scorekeeper, judge, timer) so nobody just waits.
Keep score simply, and reward good English as well as speed.
For large classes, use pairs or groups of 4 to 6, and move around to listen and note common mistakes for feedback afterwards.
End with a quick correction round: write 3 to 5 typical mistakes you heard on the board and let learners fix them.

blocks.x: Use the Classroom tools in this section (name picker, team scoreboard and timer, bingo maker and word cards) to run many of these games.

Further reading: many of these classic activities, and many more, appear in "Games for Language Learning" by Andrew Wright, David Betteridge and Michael Buckby (Cambridge University Press). The descriptions and examples in this app are written in my own words.
Listening, vocabulary (body parts, actions, classroom objects)

items: The teacher is "Simon". Learners stand up.
Give commands. Learners obey only when the command starts with "Simon says".
If you give a command without "Simon says", learners who move are out, or lose a point.
The last learners standing win. Then let a learner be Simon.
Simon says touch your nose.
Simon says point to the door.
Jump! (no "Simon says", so nobody should move)
Simon says put your pen under your chair.
Use prepositions: on, under, next to.
Speed up the commands to make it harder.
Learners take turns as Simon in small groups.

blocks.x: Teacher tip: Instead of sending learners out, give them points off, or make them judges, so nobody sits and waits.
Speaking, past tense and present perfect

items: Each learner writes three sentences about themselves: two true and one false.
In turn, a learner reads the sentences aloud.
The group asks follow-up questions, then votes on which sentence is false.
The speaker reveals the answer. Score a point for a correct guess.
I have visited three provinces. / I can play the guitar. / I have a pet snake.
I was born in the rainy season. / I have never eaten pizza. / I walked to school yesterday.
For beginners use I like / I can / I have.
Use a topic: my weekend, my childhood, my family.

blocks.x: Teacher tip: Insist on follow-up questions in full sentences: it turns a guessing game into speaking practice.
A printed or written list of prompts

items: Give each learner a list of prompts that begin with "Find someone who ...".
Learners walk around asking yes/no questions (Do you ...? Can you ...? Have you ...?).
When someone answers yes, they write that person's name next to the prompt (one name per person).
The first learner to complete the list, or the one with most names in 10 minutes, wins. Report back: "Sokha can cook."
Find someone who plays football.
Find someone who has a younger brother.
Find someone who can cook.
Find someone who likes spicy food.
Find someone who was born in the same month as you.
Use past forms: Find someone who went to the market yesterday.
Ask for a second detail: When? How often?

blocks.x: Teacher tip: Practise the questions as a class before the mingle, so learners do not just say the prompt.

items: Draw a table with categories: animals, food, jobs, countries, things in the classroom.
The teacher chooses a letter.
Teams write one word per category that begins with that letter.
The first team to finish shouts "Stop!" and everyone stops writing.
Check answers. A word no other team has scores 2 points; a shared word scores 1.
Letter B: animal: bear; food: banana; job: baker; country: Brazil; classroom: board.
Letter S: animal: snake; food: soup; job: singer; country: Spain; classroom: school bag.
Use grammar categories: a verb, an adjective, a past participle.
Add a time limit of 2 minutes instead of "Stop".

blocks.x: Teacher tip: Choose letters that have many words for beginners, and avoid X, Q and Z.

items: Learners sit or stand in a circle. The first learner says their name.
The next learner says the first name and then their own: "That is Dara, and I am Sokha."
Each learner repeats all the names before them and adds their own.
At the end, a volunteer (or the teacher) tries to say every name in the circle.
I am Dara.
That is Dara, and I am Sokha.
That is Dara, that is Sokha, and I am Vanna.
Add a gesture or an adjective that starts with the same letter: Smiling Sokha.
Add a favourite food: I am Dara and I like mangoes.

blocks.x: Teacher tip: In a big class, use several small circles so every learner gets many turns. Allow the group to help when someone forgets.
Speaking, question forms, numbers and dates

items: The teacher names something to line up by: birthdays, the distance from school, or the number of brothers and sisters.
Learners walk around and ask each other questions to find their place in the line. They may not write or show numbers.
When the line is finished, each learner says their answer in a full sentence, and the class checks the order.
Do another round with a different topic.
When is your birthday? / My birthday is on the 5th of May.
How far do you live from school? / I live two kilometres away.
How many brothers and sisters do you have?
Make two lines (or a circle) and race.
Line up in silence using only gestures.

blocks.x: Teacher tip: Model the question first, so that learners use English instead of just showing fingers.
Word cards or the Word cards tool

items: Divide the class into two teams.
One learner sees a word secretly and acts it out without speaking (or draws it, for Pictionary).
Their team guesses within 60 seconds. Score 1 point for a correct guess.
Teams take turns until everyone has acted.
Actions: brush your teeth, ride a bike, sweep the floor.
Jobs: doctor, farmer, teacher.
Feelings: tired, angry, surprised.
Phrases: give up, wake up, look for.
Pictionary: draw instead of acting.
Guess the sentence: act out a short sentence (I am eating noodles).
Teams must say the guess in a full sentence: Is it a doctor?

blocks.x: Teacher tip: Require the guessing team to speak English, with full questions, to keep the game a language activity.

items: One learner thinks of a person, animal or object and tells the teacher.
The class asks yes/no questions, up to 20, to find out what it is.
Learners can guess at any time. A correct guess wins and becomes the next thinker.
If nobody guesses after 20 questions, the thinker wins.
Is it an animal? Is it bigger than a car? Can you eat it? Does it live in water? Do we use it at school?
"Who am I?" with a name card stuck on the forehead.
Limit categories: jobs, places or foods.

blocks.x: Teacher tip: Write good question starters on the board for lower levels: Is it ...? Can you ...? Does it ...?

items: Put a chair at the front, facing the class, with its back to the board.
A learner from each team sits in the hot seat.
The teacher writes a word on the board. Teammates describe it without saying the word.
The first hot-seat learner to say the word wins a point for the team. Change learners each round.
Word: umbrella. Clues: You use it when it rains. It is round. It keeps you dry.
Word: library. Clues: You can borrow books there. It is quiet.
Allow only one-word clues for advanced learners.
Use revision vocabulary from the unit.

blocks.x: Teacher tip: Ask describers to use full sentences, and keep the volume low to avoid noise.
Cards: a target word and three forbidden words

items: Prepare cards with a target word and three forbidden words.
A learner describes the target word without using the forbidden words.
Their team guesses before time runs out (60 seconds).
Score a point for each correct guess; a forbidden word loses the card.
library: book, read, borrow
kitchen: cook, food, eat
teacher: school, class, students
bicycle: wheels, ride, pedal
Use target words from your Terminology list for teacher training.
Play with only the first three clues allowed.

blocks.x: Teacher tip: Appoint a "referee" on the other team to listen for forbidden words.
Two similar pictures per pair (Learner A and B)

items: Give Learner A and Learner B two pictures that are almost the same, with about eight differences.
Without showing each other, they describe their pictures and ask questions.
They note each difference they find.
The pair with the most differences after 10 minutes wins. Check as a class.
In my picture, there are two dogs. How many dogs are there in yours?
In mine, the man is wearing a hat. What is he wearing in yours?
Describe and draw: A describes a picture, B draws it.
Use two pictures of a house for prepositions.

blocks.x: Teacher tip: Teach the language first: There is / There are, prepositions of place, colours.

items: The teacher or a learner starts a story with one sentence.
Each learner adds one sentence to continue it.
Learners may use a word or picture card that they must include.
At the end, retell the story as a group.
Yesterday I found a strange key on the road.
Last night, I heard a noise at the door.
Each sentence must start with the next letter of the alphabet.
Each learner must use a different linking word: then, suddenly, after that.

blocks.x: Teacher tip: Praise ideas first; correct only major errors at the end, so the story keeps moving.
Speaking, asking and answering follow-up questions
Topic cards or a topic on the board

items: Give each group a topic, such as "What I did last weekend" or "A place I have visited".
One learner is the speaker. They secretly decide whether to tell the truth or invent everything.
The group asks up to eight questions to test the speaker.
The group votes: truth or lie? The speaker reveals. A fooled group gives the speaker a point; a correct group wins the point. Rotate speakers.
Where did you go? Who went with you? What did you eat? What was the weather like?
Did you see anything unusual? How did you get home?
Use a picture as the topic.
Speakers write three details first to help them stay consistent.

blocks.x: Teacher tip: Teach a few useful question starters first (Who ...? Where ...? What ...? Why ...?) and stress that asking good questions is how to win.
Speaking, guessing and speculating (could, might, must)
A picture and a sheet of paper (or a slide with a cover)

items: Cover the picture with a sheet of paper so that nothing can be seen.
Slowly slide the paper to show a small part.
Learners guess what the whole picture shows and say why.
Reveal more until someone is sure. Everyone can vote before the final reveal.
It might be an animal.
I think it is a bird because I can see a wing.
It could be a bridge, but it can't be a car.
Learners prepare their own pictures for the class.
Reveal a sentence one word at a time instead of a picture.

blocks.x: Teacher tip: Write the guess phrases on the board (It might be ... / It could be ... / It must be ...) so that learners use them.
Speaking, discussing, giving reasons, modals and conditionals
A situation card and a list of items

items: Give each group a situation: a week on an island, a trip to the mountains, or moving to a new city.
Each learner chooses three items from a list (or thinks of their own) and explains why.
The group negotiates and agrees on a final list of five items.
Groups present their list to the class and explain their reasons.
I would take a knife because we could cut wood.
We would need water first, because we can't live without it.
Do we really need a mirror? I don't think so.
Add a weight limit or a budget.
Choose items for another group.

blocks.x: Teacher tip: Let learners agree and disagree politely: Good idea. I disagree because ...
Bingo cards (use the Bingo maker tool)

items: Learners make a grid (3x3 or 4x4) and write words from a list in random squares, or the teacher prints cards.
The teacher calls words, definitions or sentences with gaps.
Learners cross out words they hear. The first to complete a line (or all) shouts "Bingo!".
Check the words the winner crossed out.
Call a definition: "You use it to write on paper." (pen)
Call a sentence: "I ___ breakfast at 6." (eat)
Call a word in the past tense: went.
Call the opposite word or the synonym.
Learners call the words in later rounds.

blocks.x: Teacher tip: Keep a tick-list of words called so you can check the winner fast.

items: A learner says a word.
The next learner says a word that starts with the last letter of the previous word.
No repeats. If a learner cannot answer in 5 seconds, they are out (or the team loses a point).
Continue until one learner or team is left.
school → lamp → pen → nose → egg → girl
Topic chain: foods only: rice → egg → grape → eel
Use a topic: foods, jobs, places.
Use the last two letters for a harder game.

blocks.x: Teacher tip: Write the words on the board to practise spelling.
Lists on the board or slides

items: Show four or five words.
Learners decide which word does not belong, and why.
They must give the reason in a full sentence.
More than one answer is allowed if the reason is good.
apple, banana, carrot, mango (carrot is a vegetable; the others are fruit)
doctor, teacher, nurse, hospital (hospital is a place, not a person)
run, jump, happy, swim (happy is an adjective, not a verb)
Learners make their own sets for other teams.
Use word families: noun, verb, adjective.

blocks.x: Teacher tip: Accept creative reasons; they show deeper thinking.
Cards in pairs (word and picture, or word and definition)

items: Mix the cards and place them face down in rows.
A learner turns over two cards.
If they match, the learner says the word in a sentence and keeps the pair; if not, the cards are turned back.
The learner with the most pairs wins.
dog + picture of a dog
happy + a smiling face
big ≠ small (opposites)
go + went (present and past)
Match a word with its definition or its synonym.
Match a verb with its past tense form.

blocks.x: Teacher tip: Ask learners to say the word aloud when they turn a card, to practise pronunciation.

items: Teams line up facing the board; the first learner in each line holds a marker.
The teacher gives a category or says a word or definition.
The first learners run to the board, write a correct word, and run back to pass the marker.
Score a point for each correct, spelled word. Continue until everyone has had a turn.
Category: write an animal that starts with C.
Definition: it is a place where you buy food (market).
Write the past tense of: go, see, eat, buy.
Teams write a whole sentence using a word.
Add a rule: no word may be used twice.

blocks.x: Teacher tip: Make sure the marker is passed; the next learner cannot start until then.
A tray of 12 to 20 objects (or a slide of pictures) and a cloth

items: Show the objects for one minute and let learners look carefully.
Cover them with a cloth or hide the slide.
Learners write as many items as they can remember.
Uncover and check. The learner (or team) with the most correct words wins.
pen, cup, key, coin, spoon, book, scissors, apple
Past tense version: There was a key. There were two coins.
Remove one object and ask which one is missing.
Ask about positions: Where was the pen? It was next to the cup.

blocks.x: Teacher tip: Choose objects from the vocabulary of your current unit.

items: Put different small objects in a bag or box.
A learner puts a hand in, feels an object without looking, and describes it.
The group guesses what it is, then the learner shows the object.
Everyone takes a turn.
It is long and hard. It is smooth. It has a point. (a pencil)
It is soft and round. (a sock or a ball)
Use smell or taste (with safe items) in other rounds.
Learners guess by feeling and say what it might be: It could be a key.

blocks.x: Teacher tip: Teach describing words before the game: soft, hard, smooth, rough, round, flat, heavy, light.

items: One learner leaves the room. The class chooses an adverb, such as slowly, angrily or quietly.
The learner returns and gives commands to others: "Walk to the door." "Open your book."
The class does each action in the manner of the adverb.
The learner guesses the adverb. Then another learner leaves.
Adverbs: slowly, quickly, angrily, sadly, happily, quietly, carefully.
Commands: Write your name. Stand up. Give me a pen.
Teams guess in turns for points.
Use adjectives instead (Mime a feeling).

blocks.x: Teacher tip: Write the list of adverbs on the board at first, so learners can choose from it.
A list of 10 to 12 sentences, some correct and some wrong; "money" (for example 1000 points per team)

items: Show a list of numbered sentences. Some are correct and some contain a grammar mistake.
Teams discuss and decide which sentences they think are correct.
Run an auction: teams bid for the sentences they think are correct.
Reveal the answers. A team gains the bid for a correct sentence and loses it for an incorrect one. The team with the most money wins.
She don't like coffee. (wrong)
He went to the market yesterday. (correct)
I have seen him last week. (wrong)
We are studying English since 2020. (wrong)
Teams must correct the wrong sentences to keep their money.
Use mistakes from your learners' own writing.

blocks.x: Teacher tip: Use real errors you collected in earlier lessons: they are the most useful for the class.

items: Write numbered sentences with one mistake each on the board, or on cards.
The first learner in each team runs to a sentence, corrects it, and returns.
The next learner takes the next sentence. Teams work through the list.
The teacher checks the answers. The fastest, correct team wins.
He go to school every day. → He goes to school every day.
There is three books on the desk. → There are three books on the desk.
I am agree with you. → I agree with you.
Each team writes mistakes for another team to correct.
Learners must explain the rule in one sentence.

blocks.x: Teacher tip: Choose mistakes from the Common Exam Errors section of the grammar handbook.

items: Cut sentences into single words and mix them in an envelope.
Learners put the words in the correct order.
The first team to finish says "Done!", reads the sentence, and the teacher checks it.
Continue with longer or harder sentences.
school / goes / she / to / every / day → She goes to school every day.
you / did / yesterday / where / go → Where did you go yesterday?
Use question forms or conditionals for higher levels.
Race with the whole class at the board.

blocks.x: Teacher tip: Let learners make scrambled sentences for other teams.

sections.title: Market Memory Chain ("I went to the market and I bought ...")

items: The first learner says: "I went to the market and I bought an apple."
The next learner repeats and adds one item: "... an apple and two eggs."
Continue around the circle. A learner who forgets an item or gets the order wrong is out.
The last learner left wins.
I went to the market and I bought rice, two fish and a bag.
Variation sentence: I packed my bag and I put in a book, a pen and a hat.
Use alphabet order for the items: apple, banana, carrot ...
Change to future: I am going to buy ...

blocks.x: Teacher tip: Write the structure on the board first, and accept help from the group.
Past simple and past continuous questions, speaking, listening
Whole class in groups of 5 or 6

items: Tell the class a mystery: a bag was stolen from the school canteen yesterday at 6 pm. Two learners (the suspects) were together.
The suspects leave the room and prepare their alibi: where they were, who they were with, and what they did. They must agree on the same story.
The other learners (detectives) prepare questions in the past tense.
The detectives interview each suspect separately and compare the answers. If the details do not match, the suspects are guilty.
What were you doing at six o'clock? Who were you with? What did you eat? What time did you leave?
What colour was the shop? How did you get home?
Change the crime and the time.
Detectives write their questions first in groups.

blocks.x: Teacher tip: Insist on detailed questions: the more details the detectives ask for, the harder it is for the suspects to keep the story.
Question forms and the future (will, going to), vocabulary
A square sheet of paper (a page cut square) and a pen

items: Fold the square in half both ways, then fold all four corners into the centre. Turn it over and fold the four corners into the centre again.
Slide a finger from each hand under the flaps so that it opens and closes. Write colours or numbers on the outside, and eight sentences or questions inside, one under each flap.
Partner A holds the fortune-teller. Partner B chooses a colour and a number. Partner A opens and closes it for each letter or number, then reads the sentence under the final flap.
Partner B answers or reacts. Swap roles.
Questions: What did you do yesterday? Where do you want to travel?
Predictions: You will meet a famous person. You will find some money.
Write irregular verb pairs inside to practise past forms.
Learners make a fortune-teller about a theme from your unit.

blocks.x: Teacher tip: Fold one yourself on the board first. Folding takes time, so keep the sentences short.
Prepositions of place, questions and short answers
A drawing of a room (or a table with objects) and a small paper mouse

items: Draw a simple room or a picture with furniture on the board.
One learner writes down where the mouse is hiding, such as under the table.
Other learners ask yes/no questions, such as "Is it under the table?" until someone guesses.
The winner hides the mouse next.
Is it in the box? No, it isn't.
Is it behind the chair? Yes, it is!
Pairs do it with their own drawn pictures.
Ask in the past: Where was the mouse? It was on the shelf.

blocks.x: Teacher tip: Teach the prepositions first: in, on, under, behind, next to, between, in front of.
A short text (4 to 8 sentences) stuck on the wall or outside the room

items: Put the text on the wall, far from the teams.
One runner reads and remembers a sentence, runs back, and dictates it to the writer.
Learners swap roles after each sentence.
The first team to write all sentences correctly wins. Check spelling and accuracy.
My brother likes football. He plays every Saturday with his friends.
Dara buys fruit from the market in the morning.
Use a text with the key vocabulary from your unit.
Add a mistake in the text for the team to find.

blocks.x: Teacher tip: Make clear that accuracy matters, not only speed.

items: Learners stand in a line. The first learner reads a sentence on a slip.
They whisper it once to the next learner, who whispers it onward.
The last learner says the sentence aloud to the class.
Compare the first and last versions, and discuss where it changed.
The sheep jumped over the six white fences.
She sells sea shells by the sea shore.
I would like a cup of tea with two sugars.
Use a longer sentence for a harder game.
Add a rule: only say it once.

blocks.x: Teacher tip: Use the funny results to practise stress and clear pronunciation.

items: One learner describes a picture or a scene.
The other learner draws what they hear, without seeing the original.
They compare drawings with the original and discuss differences.
Swap roles.
There is a house in the middle. There is a tree on the left. The sun is above the house.
Draw a circle. Draw a square next to it. Put a star under the circle.
The teacher describes and the whole class draws.
Use a map or room layout.

blocks.x: Teacher tip: Pre-teach the key prepositions and colours before the game.

sections.title: Repeat It If It Is True

items: The teacher says a sentence.
If it is true, learners repeat it. If it is false, they stay silent (or say "No!" and correct it).
Increase the speed and make the sentences closer to the truth.
Let learners take over as the teacher.
A cat has four legs.
The sun is cold.
Water boils at 100 degrees.
We have English lessons on Sundays.
Use sentences about the learners themselves: Dara has a red bag.
Add grammar errors to false sentences and ask learners to correct them.

blocks.x: Teacher tip: Use the content of your last unit to make the sentences, so it doubles as revision.
Two versions of a short text

items: Read a short text aloud. Then read it again with several small changes.
Learners write or raise a hand each time they hear a change.
Read a third time and discuss the differences.
Pairs can take turns reading changed texts to each other.
She has two brothers and lives near the school. / She has three brothers and lives near the school.
I went to the market on Monday. / I went to the market on Sunday.
Minimal pairs: ship / sheep, bed / bad.
Change only one sound to practise pronunciation.
Hand out the text and let learners find what was changed.

blocks.x: Teacher tip: Start with large changes and make them smaller as the class improves.

items: Teach the key actions with gestures.
Tell a short story slowly while learners act it out.
Repeat faster, then let learners tell the story while others act.
Finally, ask learners to retell the story in the past tense.
I wake up. I open the window. I wash my face. I eat breakfast. I go to school.
The farmer takes a bucket. He walks to the river. He fills the bucket.
Groups act different parts of one story.
Add a mistake in the story and learners stop and correct it.

blocks.x: Teacher tip: Say each sentence twice and pause, so learners can match action to words.
Story cut into sentence strips (one set per group)

items: Cut a short story into separate sentences and mix them.
Groups read the strips and put them in order.
Read the story aloud (or let a group read) and the groups check their order.
Ask which words helped them decide: first, then, after that, finally.
Mina got up late. / She missed the bus. / She ran to school. / She arrived after the bell. / The teacher smiled and let her in.
Use pictures instead of sentences.
The teacher reads the story only once while groups arrange it.

blocks.x: Teacher tip: Write the linking words on the board first (first, then, after that, finally).

items: Think of a word and draw a dash for each letter on the board.
Learners call a letter. If it is in the word, write it in the correct place.
If not, draw one part of the hangman (or use another picture, such as a flower losing petals).
The class wins by guessing the word before the drawing is complete.
_ _ _ _ _ _ (teacher)
Topic: animals. Word: elephant.
Use sentences, not words.
Teams take turns choosing words for other teams.

blocks.x: Teacher tip: Pick a gentler picture than a hangman, such as a tree growing leaves, if you prefer.

items: Learners choose a topic, such as their town, a text they just read, or their own life.
Each writes six sentences: three true and three false.
Partners swap papers, mark each sentence true or false, and correct the false ones.
Discuss the answers together.
My school has a library. / My school has a swimming pool.
The text says that tsunamis are caused by tides. (false)
Dictate the sentences instead of swapping papers.
Write true and false definitions of words.

blocks.x: Teacher tip: Use texts you have already read in class: it checks reading comprehension too.

items: Each learner writes the first line on their paper: a man or woman (a name and description), then folds the paper so the line is hidden and passes it on.
On the next paper they receive, they write the next line: where they met. Fold and pass again.
Continue with: what the first person said; what the second person said; what they did; and what happened in the end.
Unfold the papers and read the stories aloud. They are usually funny.
A tall woman called Sokha... / met a farmer called Dara... / in the market... / She said, "Do you like noodles?"... / He said, "No, I like rice."... / They shared a bowl... / and the market closed.
Use past simple only.
Write a different line each time, such as why and how.

blocks.x: Teacher tip: Write the list of prompts on the board so everybody knows what to write next.

items: Each learner writes the first sentence of a story at the top of a sheet.
After one minute, learners pass the sheet to the right.
The next learner reads it, then adds one more sentence. Keep passing until each sheet returns to its owner.
The group reads its stories aloud and picks one to tell the class.
On Monday morning I found a letter on my bed.
It was raining when the old man opened the door.
Each learner adds a paragraph instead of a sentence.
Include three words that the teacher chooses.

blocks.x: Teacher tip: Give a short time limit for each pass so the stories keep moving.
A list or picture of items found in a pocket

items: Show a list of objects found in a person's pocket (for example a key, a ticket, a photo, a coin).
Groups imagine who the person is: age, job, personality, and what the day was like.
Each group writes a short description using might, must and could.
Groups read their descriptions aloud. The class decides which story is the most believable.
He might be a teacher because he has a red pen.
He must have travelled by bus because he has a ticket.
She could be a student; she has a library card.
Give each group different objects.
Use a handbag, a school bag or a pencil case.

blocks.x: Teacher tip: Pre-teach "must have" and "might have" for deductions about the past.

items: Write a key word in a circle in the middle of the page and draw rays around it, like the sun.
On each ray, write a word that goes with the key word: a verb, an adjective, a thing or a phrase.
Colour-code the types of word, and add a sentence at the end.
Compare with a partner and add new words.
market: fruit, buy, cheap, crowded, price, sell

items: Fold a sheet of paper in half lengthwise, then in half twice more to make eight sections. Unfold it.
Fold it in half the other way, and cut a slit along the middle fold between the two centre sections.
Push the ends together so the slit opens, and fold the paper into a small eight-page booklet.
On each page, write a new word, a short meaning, and an example sentence. Add a small drawing.
Page: reduce. Meaning: make smaller. Example: We must reduce the noise.
Page: borrow. Meaning: take and return later. Example: I borrow books from the library.
Make one booklet per unit.
Swap booklets with a partner and test each other.

blocks.x: Teacher tip: Show learners how to fold it once in class. A tiny book is easy to carry and use on the bus.
Board with a category grid and point values (100, 200, 300, 400)

items: Draw a grid on the board: categories across the top and point values below.
A team chooses a category and a value; the teacher reads the question.
The team answers within 20 seconds. Correct answers win the points; wrong ones lose them.
The team with the most points at the end wins.
Grammar 100: Choose: She ___ to school every day. (go / goes)

items: Each learner gets a card with a question on one side and the answer on the other.
Learners walk around and find a partner.
Partner A asks the question; partner B answers. Then swap roles. The asker gives help if needed.
They trade cards and find a new partner. Repeat for 10 minutes.
